passage:
Dear Arohi,

I owe you an update, and I think you will be surprised. We pulled the usage data for the clinic app last week. Of everything we built, the billing screens, the notes, the dashboards, hardly anyone touches anything except the appointment reminder. The rest sits untouched. My first reaction was to defend the other features, because we spent a year on them. Then I asked myself what our users actually come back for. The reminder is the real product. Everything else is packaging. So next month we will strip the app down to reminders, do them really well, and see whether clinics will pay for that alone. I would love an hour of your time to think about pricing.

Lakshmi

passage:
Jahnavi, the turning point wasn't a brainstorm. It was a boring chart. I'm Harish; our clinic app had everything: booking, billing, patient notes, a chat, a health tips section. Eighteen months of work. One Sunday I finally opened the usage data properly. Nearly every clinic used exactly one thing: the SMS reminder before an appointment. Billing? Hardly touched. Notes? Two clinics. Health tips? Nobody.
I sat there and thought it through. Why do they keep paying? Because no-shows cost them money, and the reminder fixes that. Everything else we built, they already had some other way. So the reminder isn't a feature of our product. The reminder is the product. The rest was decoration we had fallen in love with.
That was hard to admit, Jahnavi. But it made the next step obvious.

qa.q: What was the one thing nearly every clinic used?
qa.a: The SMS reminder before an appointment.

qa.q: How did Harish feel admitting the rest was decoration?
qa.a: Harish felt uncomfortable and a little sad to admit it, then relieved once the next step became obvious.

qa.q: What could Harish's team do next with this insight?
qa.a: Make the reminder excellent and simple, and ask clinics what would make it more useful, before cutting the rest.

qa.q: How might the clinics see a product focused on reminders?
qa.a: Clinics would likely welcome it, since the reminder is what saves them from no-shows.

grounding: It shows a founder reading usage data, seeing that almost everyone uses only the appointment reminder, and reasoning that it is the real product.

I sit next to the product team at our salon-software startup, so I watched Gurpreet the week the numbers came in. The dashboard showed that almost every salon used one thing: the reminder message sent to customers the day before an appointment. Stock tracking, staff rota, loyalty points: barely touched.
Gurpreet printed the chart and taped it to the wall. For two days I saw Gurpreet standing in front of it, arms folded, saying things aloud like, "They pay for the reminder. The rest is what we thought they wanted." On Thursday, in the team meeting, Gurpreet said, "I think the reminder is the product. Everything else is decoration." The designer who built loyalty points looked hurt.
I can't say whether it was easy for Gurpreet to say. But by Friday the roadmap on the whiteboard had one word circled: reminders.
— Harsha

qa.a: Acknowledge the work openly and involve the designer in making the reminder product better.

qa.a: The designer looked hurt, since the feature they built was now called decoration.
